newsitem.title: UK: UK ethnic minorities enjoy mixed success - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK ethnic minorities enjoy mixed success - survey.

text.p: Forty years after they first arrived in Britain, Chinese and African Asian minorities are enjoying a standard of living comparable to the white population, a survey released on Wednesday showed.
But other ethnic groups still face serious disadvantage, with Pakistanis and Bangladeshis experiencing the greatest poverty.

"The main conclusion is that there is a diversity in the ethnic groups covered in the survey. The distance between them is as important as the similarities," said Tariq Modood, programme director at the Policy Studies Institute which conducted the survey.
Of the three million people making up Britain's ethnic minorities, those to enjoy the most economic success were African Asians -- Indians whose parents had lived in Africa -- and Chinese minorities.
Much of this success came through self-employment which generated above average incomes and made up for under representation in top business jobs.
"All groups of minority men are under represented in top company jobs," said Modood.
But he added: "More than four-fifths of Pakistani and Bangladeshi households are in poverty. They are four times as likely to be below the government's definition of poverty."
And the African Caribbean ethnic group, which at 500,000 is Britain's largest ethnic group, was another major sufferer.

Half the families in that group were headed by a lone parent and they were more likely to be in poverty than whites or Chinese. Unemployment among African Caribbeans male was as high as 50 percent in many areas.
"It is not normal to have a job in these groups, it is just as normal not to have one," said Richard Berthoud, who led the survey team.
The survey was based on interviews with more than 5,000 people of Caribbean, South Asian and Chinese origin and almost 3,000 white people.
While education was identified as having a positive impact on socio-economic circumstances among most ethnic minorities, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis were not following this trend.
"A Pakistani or a Bangladeshi with a degree is just as likely to live below the poverty line as a white person with no qualifications," said Berthoud.

The survey also found that, 40 years after widespread immigration from the Caribbean and the Indian sub-continent started, racism was still entrenched in Britain. More than 250,000 British Asians experience racial harassment each year, said Modood.
"White people still admit to being prejudiced against ethnic minorities and young whites are more likely to say they are prejudiced against Asian minorites," he said.
The survey did not set out policy recommendations for Britain's new Labour government but Berthoud said he hoped it would take note of the findings and put a premium on education.

Berthoud urged the government to treat minority groups with the individual attention they each required and specified the need to provide English lessons for those who had not yet crossed the first hurdle to improving their situation.
